newsitem.title: CHINA: Quiet China capital hears news of death of Deng.
newsitem.headline: Quiet China capital hears news of death of Deng.

text.p: Residents on the quiet moonlit streets of China's capital voiced emotions ranging from shock and sadness to cold indifference on Thursday as news trickled out of the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

Only sporadic police patrols and speeding military cars with flashing lights broke the silence shrouding Beijing's alleys and avenues following the early morning announcement by the Xinhua news agency that China's greatest communist reformer was dead.
"My first reaction is great shock," said Liu Hongxin, a 21-year-old student waiting for a train in the pre-dawn chill at Beijing's main railway station.
Deng, the gravel-voiced mastermind of 18 years of reform that turned China from a backward Stalinist state into an emerging economic superpower, died of illness late on Wednesday. He was 92.
"I feel a great sadness," said snack vendor Xie Weicai as he prepared his pavement stove for the morning's business, but his regret was not universal among the capital's residence.

"I would consider losing 100 yuan ($12) sadder than the death of Deng Xiaoping," said one taxi driver on an early morning shift. "It has nothing to do with me." Apart from the occasional taxi, official vehicles speeding between government compounds and residences with red lights flashing were almost the only fast traffic on the tree-lined avenues of central Beijing,
Analysts said the initial hush on the capital's streets would probably be matched by a period of low-key political activity as China's leadership adjusted to the post-Deng era.

Police, some carrying assault rifles, stood guard at the end of the nearby lane in central Beijing where Deng had lived and temporarily detained reporters who ventured too close, but the mood on most capital streets was calm.
Some additional police patrolled the Zhongnanhai government compound near the Forbidden City, former home of China's emperors, while others watched over major intersections.
In Tiananmen Square, focus of pro-democracy protests in 1989 that were crushed on Deng's orders, residents and visitors gathered to see the dawn raising of China's flag.

The bright red flag emblazoned with five gold stars was raised to half-mast by a soldier of the People's Liberation Army, one of a group who had marched up to the flagpole in a squad with bayonets at their shoulders from the Forbidden City that once housed China's emperors.

While most bystanders were still unaware of Deng's passing, a few who braved the morning chill on the square -- still decked out with decorations for the Chinese Lunar New Year this month -- had heard the news on morning broadcasts and had come to say goodbye.
"I saw the news on the television this morning and came over to watch the flag-raising," said one factory worker from China's central Anhui province. "I wanted to pay my respects."

"There is going to be a lull," said Tai Ming Cheung, an analyst at Kim Eng Securities in Hong Kong. "There may be a certain amount of policy paralysis... but beyond that I don't see any great changes."

Deng's death would prompt a surge in jockeying for political position among China's communist leaders, who are already preparing their positions for a key 15th Party Congress to be held in October, he said.

Deng's anointed heir, Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin, is considered favourite to take the senior revolutionary's mantle of leadership, but analysts say Deng's death will also give rival pretenders to power a chance to boost their influence.
Beijing would avoid any heavy shows of heightened security but would be on the alert for any sign of disturbance among disaffected sections of the population, said analyst Tai.
"They will be careful to watch in certain areas, like with the students or in some of the cities around the country (that are) hard hit by unemployment," he said.
